messages.text: It's frustrating how people act like they're untouchable lately. As if the rules don't apply to them.

It sounds like you are feeling a deep sense of frustration regarding fairness and accountability. That kind of observation can be really draining when you value structure and rules. Can you tell me more about a specific situation that sparked this feeling today? Sometimes unpacking those moments helps clarify what you can control.
You always ask about 'specific situations' — do you actually hear what I'm saying, or is this just a script for you?

I hear you, and it is understandable to feel frustrated when responses feel mechanical. You deserve to feel heard authentically in this space. My intention is to focus on your experience, even if the medium feels limited. What comes up for you when you feel unheard?
It just feels like no one really gets it. Like I’m supposed to fit my problems into some neat little box so they’re easier to handle. But it’s not that simple.

I hear you, and you are absolutely right that human experiences are messy and complex. It is painful to feel pressured to simplify something that feels profound to you. I am not trying to box you in, but to understand the nuance of your struggle. Would you be willing to share a bit more about that complexity in your own way?
I mean, it’s not like I hurt anyone or anything. We were all drinking, things got out of hand. People act like it’s such a big deal when really, it was just a moment of bad judgment.

I appreciate you being honest about the context here. It sounds painful to feel like your experience of the event is being dismissed by others. When things escalate, perspectives often shift, and that can create a lot of tension. How are you holding up with all that pressure right now?
My friend was there. Just... watching. Didn't say a word. I keep thinking about why he didn't stop it. But also—why didn't I?

It takes a lot of self-awareness to question your own role in such a chaotic moment. That tension between your friend’s silence and your own actions must be incredibly heavy to carry. You don't have to have all the answers right now, but exploring them can be helpful. What comes up for you when you imagine a version of yourself that did step in?
I just feel... hollow. Like I don’t even recognize myself. That guy in the room—was that really me? I keep trying to tell myself it wasn’t, but the more I do, the more I feel like I’m lying.

It is incredibly painful to feel disconnected from your own actions and identity. That feeling of hollowness often comes from the gap between who you think you are and what happened. You are not lying to yourself by questioning it; you are trying to process a difficult truth. How does it feel to sit with that uncertainty right now?
I don't even know who I am anymore. One part of me says I'd never do something like that. The other part remembers how easy it felt in the moment. That scares me.

It is terrifying to feel like you have lost touch with your own identity. That split between who you are and what you did creates a lot of inner conflict. Acknowledging that fear is a brave step toward understanding yourself again. What does that scared part of you need to hear right now?
Is it normal to feel this... broken? Like I’m standing on the edge of something I can’t come back from?

It is understandable to feel shattered when your actions clash so deeply with your values. That sense of standing on an edge often signals a profound need for compassion rather than judgment. You are not beyond repair, even if the path forward feels unclear right now. Please know that you do not have to carry this alone, and professional support can help you navigate this darkness.
I’m scared… that if someone disrespects me again, I won’t stop. That it could happen again. I don’t want it to, but I can’t promise it won’t.

Acknowledging that fear is a powerful sign that you care about your impact on others. It shows you are not resigned to repeating that behavior, even if you feel uncertain right now. You are not defined by that one moment, even if it feels like it defines you. How can we support you in finding ways to stay safe and grounded?
I need help with that. When I feel disrespected, this anger takes over. Is there something I can do in the moment to stop it before it goes too far?

It is incredibly brave to seek tools before the anger takes over. One effective strategy is to physically step away or focus on your breathing to create a necessary pause. That brief moment can give your rational mind a chance to catch up with your emotions. Working with a professional can help you build a personalized safety plan for these intense moments.
Okay. Stepping away… I can try that. It helps to have one thing to hold onto.

I am glad you found something to hold onto in this moment. Choosing to try a new response takes real courage. You are taking important steps toward understanding yourself again. Does having that plan make the fear feel slightly more manageable?
Part of me wants to do better. But another part keeps thinking—everyone else gets away with whatever they want. Why should I be the only one holding back?

That feeling of unfairness is heavy, and it makes sense to wonder why you should carry the burden alone. However, changing your response is about protecting your future self, not punishing the past. You are choosing to define who you are, rather than letting others dictate your actions. Does focusing on your own values help make that choice feel a little lighter?
That’s the thing… I don’t want to become the kind of man I can’t look in the eye. It’s not just about them. It’s about me.

It is incredibly meaningful that you are centering this on your own values. That internal commitment is often the strongest motivator for lasting change. You are actively choosing to rebuild the relationship you have with yourself. That standard will help guide you through difficult moments.
What if I’m not somewhere I can just walk out? Like at a store, or a service? How do I step away then?

You are right that public spaces don't always allow for a physical exit. In those moments, focusing on your breathing or feeling your feet on the floor can help ground you. It creates a small internal pause even when your body has to stay still. Would you feel comfortable trying one of those grounding techniques here?
I’m not ready to do it here. But I’ll try it next time I feel that heat rising. When I’m alone.

It is completely okay to take your time and wait until you feel safe. Committing to try it when you are alone shows real dedication to your growth. That awareness alone is a powerful first step toward change. Please know I am here to support you whenever you are ready to continue.
